title: THE TAX COLLECTOR WHO WALKED AWAY FROM MONEY: How Do We Know Matthew Was Wealthy?
paragraphs:
THE TAX COLLECTOR WHO WALKED AWAY FROM MONEY: How Do We Know Matthew Was Wealthy?
The Bible never tells us Matthew’s bank balance. But one dinner, one Greek word, one abandoned booth, and two words from Jesus reveal something far more important than how much money he had: what happened when a man who had learned how to profit from this world finally discovered Someone worth losing everything for.
There was money on the table.
Maybe a lot of it.
Coins changing hands. Goods passing through. Merchants waiting. Travelers calculating what they owed.
And sitting in the middle of that machinery was a man named Matthew.
Then Jesus walked by.
No lengthy negotiation.
No carefully prepared discipleship contract.
No promise that Matthew would become famous.
No guarantee of comfort.
Just a command:
“Follow Me.”
And Matthew stood up.
That sounds simple until you understand what he was standing up from.
Because when Jesus called fishermen, they could conceivably return to their boats.
Matthew was sitting at something very different.
The Greek text of Matthew 9:9 describes him as:
“ἐπὶ τὸ τελώνιον”
epi to telōnion — at the tax booth, the toll or customs office.
The word τελώνιον (telōnion) refers to the place where tolls, customs, or taxes were collected.
Matthew was not introduced to us begging beside the road.
He was not introduced as a fisherman repairing torn nets.
He was sitting at a revenue station.
And that matters.
But we need to be careful here, because Christians should never make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
The Bible never gives Matthew’s net worth.
It never says, “Matthew was a rich man.”
It never tells us how many coins he owned, how large his property was, or how much money he earned in a year.
So saying with absolute certainty that Matthew was extraordinarily wealthy would go beyond the biblical evidence.
But Scripture does give us clues that Matthew—also identified with Levi in the parallel Gospel accounts—possessed meaningful financial resources.
And one of the strongest clues appears almost immediately after Jesus calls him.
Luke records the moment this way:
“Καὶ καταλιπὼν πάντα ἀναστὰς ἠκολούθει αὐτῷ.”
Leaving everything, he rose and followed Him.
Everything.
Luke does not merely tell us Matthew changed careers.
He tells us something was left behind.
Then comes a fascinating detail.
Matthew throws a banquet.
Not merely a private meal.
Not bread for Jesus and a few friends.
Luke describes it as:
“δοχὴν μεγάλην”
dochēn megalēn.
A great banquet.
And it happened in Matthew’s own house.
A large crowd was there, including many tax collectors and others.
Think about that scene.
Tables.
Food.
Guests.
A house capable of receiving them.
A host capable of providing for them.
Matthew had apparently accumulated enough resources to host a significant gathering, and enough social influence within his former world that many people came.
That does not allow us to calculate his wealth.
But it certainly suggests that Matthew was not destitute.
There is another clue hidden in his occupation.

Tax collectors occupied a deeply controversial place in first-century Jewish society. They handled revenue within a political and economic system hated by many of their fellow Jews. Tax collection could provide opportunities for profit and abuse, which helps explain why “tax collectors and sinners” appear together so frequently in the Gospel narratives.
But we should also resist turning Matthew into a criminal when Scripture never explicitly tells us that he personally cheated anyone.
Zacchaeus speaks about restoring anything obtained through fraud.
Matthew does not.
The Gospel calls Matthew a tax collector.
That alone carried enormous social stigma.
But Scripture does not give us permission to invent sins for him.
And this is where Matthew's story becomes more uncomfortable than a simplistic tale about a greedy rich man.
Because perhaps the deepest scandal was not merely what Matthew had done.
It was who Jesus was willing to call.
Imagine Matthew sitting behind that booth.
People knew him.
People had opinions about him.
Some probably despised him before he ever opened his mouth.
Maybe he had money...
but money cannot make people love you.
Maybe he had influence...
but influence cannot silence shame.
Maybe his house could hold a crowd...
but a crowded house does not guarantee an unlonely heart.
You can own things and still feel owned by them.
You can make money and quietly wonder what your life is worth.
You can smile in photographs, pay your bills, build your career, buy another thing you once prayed to afford...
and still lie awake wondering:
Is this really all there is?
That is where Matthew's story stops being ancient history.
Because somewhere inside many of us sits a tax booth.
Not literally.
But there is something we are afraid Jesus might ask us to leave.
A relationship.
An addiction.
A secret.
An image.
A career that has become an idol.
Money.
Pornography.
Pride.
Bitterness.
The approval of people.
A hidden compromise nobody at church knows about.
We want Jesus...
but we would prefer Him not to touch the booth.
We want salvation without surrender.
Grace without repentance.
A Savior who forgives us, but preferably not a Lord who tells us to get up.
Then Jesus walks straight toward the place we thought He would avoid.
And He says:
Follow Me.
Notice what He did not say.
“Matthew, clean yourself up first.”
“Matthew, repair your reputation.”
“Matthew, prove you deserve another chance.”
“Matthew, explain every mistake you have ever made.”
Jesus called him.
And Matthew got up.
That is grace.
But do not confuse grace with permission to remain unchanged.
The grace that found Matthew at the booth called Matthew away from the booth.
That distinction matters desperately in a generation that sometimes wants Jesus as Savior while resisting Jesus as Lord.
Biblical grace does not say your sin does not matter.
Biblical grace says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross for it—and His mercy is so powerful that your sin no longer has to own you.
Jesus would later explain why He was sitting with people like Matthew:
“I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.”
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Jesus does not wait at a distance for sinners to become respectable enough to approach Him.
He enters their world.
He calls them.
He eats with them.
And ultimately He goes to a cross for them.
But there is something beautiful about Matthew's first response that we can easily miss.
What does this former tax collector do with his resources after encountering Jesus?
He opens his home.
He fills his table.
And he brings people from his old world close enough to encounter Christ.
Read that again.
The house that could have represented Matthew's success became a place where sinners encountered Jesus.
The resources that could have served Matthew's status became instruments of hospitality.
The relationships attached to his former life became a mission field.
Matthew did not merely walk away from something.
He began using what remained for Someone.
And perhaps that is the question this story has been moving toward all along.
Not:
How wealthy was Matthew?
But:
Who owns what you have?
Your house.
Your money.
Your business.
Your audience.
Your influence.
Your phone.
Your voice.
Your gifts.
Your time.
Your story.
If Jesus has rewritten your life, what would happen if the things that once existed primarily for you became places where other people encountered Him?
That is why sharing the Gospel should never merely be an algorithmic exercise.
It can be worship.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
God's approval cannot be purchased.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith.”
We support Gospel work not to earn salvation, but because salvation has already produced gratitude.
So if you genuinely want to glorify God through the resources and influence He has entrusted to you, consider helping Gospel truth travel farther.
Send it privately to someone sitting at their own invisible tax booth.
Maybe their story is one encounter with Jesus away from being rewritten.
Be honest.
There is no shame in needing prayer.
Matthew's story exists because Jesus specializes in calling people nobody expected Him to call.
There may come a day when the thing you are tempted to return to starts calling your name again.
Come back and remember the tax booth.
Remember the banquet.
Remember the command.
Follow Me.

We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, spiritual nourishment, repentance, grace, and the relentless announcement that Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
It is not a payment to God.
It is not a shortcut to blessing.
It is not proof that you are a better Christian.
Christ alone saves.
But financial support can help Gospel ministry continue reaching people, just as believers throughout Scripture willingly used material resources to serve the work of God.
But before you leave, return to Matthew.
The coins are still on the table.
The booth is still standing.
People are still passing by.
And the man who used to sit there is walking away.
Can you see him?
He does not know everything that following Jesus will cost.
He does not know every road ahead.
He does not know every argument, every miracle, every storm, every failure among the disciples, every bewildering moment still waiting for them.
He only knows who called him.
And somehow...
that is enough.
This is what makes Matthew's possible prosperity interesting but ultimately secondary.
The miracle is not that a man may have possessed significant resources.
The miracle is that when Jesus became more precious than what he possessed, he got up.
The scandal was the tax collector.
The grace was Jesus walking toward him.
The transformation was Matthew walking away with Jesus.
And eventually the story of a despised tax collector would become inseparable from the proclamation of a King whose kingdom cannot be bought.
Maybe you have spent years building your booth.
Maybe yours has a different name.
Success.
Pleasure.
Reputation.
Control.
Religion.
Comfort.
Secret sin.
Maybe nobody else recognizes it.
Jesus does.
And still...
He comes near.
Not because your sin is small.
Not because holiness does not matter.
Not because repentance is optional.
He comes because sinners are exactly the people He came to save.
At the cross, Jesus Christ bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the same Christ who called Matthew still calls sinners today—not merely toward improved behavior, but toward Himself.
So the greatest question is no longer:
Was Matthew wealthy?
The evidence suggests he had meaningful means, but Scripture does not give us enough information to calculate his wealth with certainty.
The greater question is:
What could Matthew possibly have possessed that was worth more than Jesus?
Nothing.
Neither do we.
And comment—not for an algorithm, but as an act of spiritual honesty:
“Jesus, I will follow You.”
Because somewhere right now, another Matthew is still sitting behind another booth...
and Jesus is still calling sinners to get up.
The world may remember where you were sitting. Jesus is writing the story of where you go after you stand.
